<div class="container">
    <header>
        <div class="breadcrumb">
            <a href="/">Home</a> / <a href="/guides/">Guides</a> / Threat Hunting Techniques
        </div>
        <h1>Threat Hunting Techniques<span class="new-badge">NEW</span></h1>
        <div class="meta">
            <div class="meta-item">📅 Published: Dec 13, 2025</div>
            <div class="meta-item">⏱️ 20 min read</div>
            <div class="meta-item">🏷️ Advanced</div>
        </div>
    </header>

    <article class="content">
        <img src="/images/guides/threat-hunting-techniques.png"
            alt="Threat Hunting Techniques & Methodologies Guide" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <p>Threat hunting is where security gets proactive. Instead of waiting for alerts to fire, you go looking
            for adversaries who have already bypassed your defenses. It's detective work—forming hypotheses,
            collecting evidence, and finding what others missed.</p>

        <p>I've spent countless hours hunting through logs, and here's what I've learned: <strong>the best threat
                hunters aren't the ones with the most tools—they're the ones who think like attackers and understand
                their environment deeply.</strong></p>

        <div class="callout purple">
            <strong>Threat Hunting vs. Incident Response:</strong> IR is reactive—you respond to alerts. Hunting is
            proactive—you assume you're already compromised and search for evidence. The goal is to find threats
            that evaded detection.
        </div>

        <h2>1. The Threat Hunting Process</h2>

        <div class="process-flow">
            <div class="process-step active">Hypothesis</div>
            <span class="process-arrow">→</span>
            <div class="process-step">Data Collection</div>
            <span class="process-arrow">→</span>
            <div class="process-step">Analysis</div>
            <span class="process-arrow">→</span>
            <div class="process-step">Findings</div>
            <span class="process-arrow">→</span>
            <div class="process-step">Improve Defenses</div>
        </div>

        <h3>Step 1: Form a Hypothesis</h3>
        <p>Every hunt starts with a question. Good hypotheses are:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Specific:</strong> "Attackers may be using PowerShell to download malware" vs. "There might
                be malware"</li>
            <li><strong>Testable:</strong> Can be proven or disproven with available data</li>
            <li><strong>Threat-informed:</strong> Based on real TTPs used by adversaries</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Step 2: Collect Data</h3>
        <p>Identify what data sources you need:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Endpoint:</strong> Process execution, file creation, registry changes</li>
            <li><strong>Network:</strong> DNS queries, HTTP requests, flow data</li>
            <li><strong>Authentication:</strong> Logon events, privilege usage</li>
            <li><strong>Application:</strong> Web server logs, database queries</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Step 3: Analyze</h3>
        <p>Look for patterns, anomalies, and indicators:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Statistical outliers (rare processes, unusual connections)</li>
            <li>Known-bad indicators (IOCs)</li>
            <li>Behavioral patterns (sequences of actions)</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Step 4: Document Findings</h3>
        <p>Whether you find a threat or not, document:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>The hypothesis tested</li>
            <li>Data sources and queries used</li>
            <li>Findings (true positive, false positive, or inconclusive)</li>
            <li>Recommendations</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Step 5: Improve Defenses</h3>
        <p>Turn hunts into detections:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Create automated alerts for confirmed TTPs</li>
            <li>Update detection rules</li>
            <li>Identify visibility gaps</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>2. Hypothesis Generation Sources</h2>

        <p>Where do good hunting hypotheses come from?</p>

        <h3>Threat Intelligence</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>APT reports:</strong> What TTPs are threat groups using?</li>
            <li><strong>Industry-specific threats:</strong> What's targeting your sector?</li>
            <li><strong>Emerging threats:</strong> New malware, zero-days, attack techniques</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>MITRE ATT&CK Framework</h3>
        <p>The ATT&CK framework is a threat hunter's best friend. It catalogs adversary tactics and techniques with
            real-world examples.</p>

        <div class="callout info">
            <strong>ATT&CK Tactics (Kill Chain):</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem;">
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Reconnaissance</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Initial Access</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Execution</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Persistence</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Privilege Escalation</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Defense Evasion</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Credential Access</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Discovery</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Lateral Movement</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Collection</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Exfiltration</span>
                <span class="mitre-tactic">Command & Control</span>
            </p>
        </div>

        <h3>Environmental Knowledge</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>What's normal?</strong> Baseline behaviors for your environment</li>
            <li><strong>What's valuable?</strong> Crown jewels that attract attackers</li>
            <li><strong>What's vulnerable?</strong> Known weaknesses, unpatched systems</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Past Incidents</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>How did past attackers get in?</li>
            <li>What TTPs were used?</li>
            <li>Are there similar patterns still occurring?</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>3. Hunting Techniques</h2>

        <h3>Technique 1: IOC-Based Hunting</h3>
        <p>Search for known-bad indicators—hashes, IPs, domains, file names.</p>

        <div class="hunt-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Hunt: Known Malware Hashes</h5>
            <p><strong>Hypothesis:</strong> Malware from recent APT campaign may be present in our environment.</p>
            <pre><code># Splunk - Search for known bad hashes

index=endpoint (hash=e99a18c428cb38d5f260853678922e03 OR hash=5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592) | table _time, host, file_path, hash, user 

        <p><strong>Pros:</strong> Quick, easy, specific<br>
            <strong>Cons:</strong> Only finds known threats; attackers can change IOCs easily
        </p>

        <h3>Technique 2: TTP-Based Hunting</h3>
        <p>Search for adversary behaviors rather than specific indicators.</p>

        <div class="hunt-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Hunt: PowerShell Download Cradles</h5>
            <p><strong>Hypothesis:</strong> Attackers may use PowerShell to download and execute payloads.</p>
            <p><span class="mitre-tactic">Execution</span> <span class="mitre-technique">T1059.001 -
                    PowerShell</span></p>
            <pre><code># Splunk - PowerShell download patterns

index=windows EventCode=4688 New_Process_Name=“powershell.exe” (Process_Command_Line=“downloadstring” OR Process_Command_Line=“downloadfile” OR Process_Command_Line=“invoke-webrequest” OR Process_Command_Line=“wget” OR Process_Command_Line=“curl” OR Process_Command_Line=“Net.WebClient”) | table _time, host, user, Process_Command_Line 

        <div class="hunt-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Hunt: Suspicious Parent-Child Process Relationships</h5>
            <p><strong>Hypothesis:</strong> Malicious documents spawn unexpected child processes.</p>
            <p><span class="mitre-tactic">Execution</span> <span class="mitre-technique">T1204 - User
                    Execution</span></p>
            <pre><code># Splunk - Office spawning suspicious children

index=windows EventCode=4688 (Parent_Process_Name=“WINWORD.EXE” OR Parent_Process_Name=“EXCEL.EXE” OR Parent_Process_Name=“OUTLOOK.EXE”) (New_Process_Name=“cmd.exe” OR New_Process_Name=“powershell.exe” OR New_Process_Name=“wscript.exe” OR New_Process_Name=“mshta.exe” OR New_Process_Name=“certutil.exe”) | table _time, host, user, Parent_Process_Name, New_Process_Name, Process_Command_Line 

        <h3>Technique 3: Anomaly-Based Hunting</h3>
        <p>Find statistical outliers—things that deviate from normal.</p>

        <div class="hunt-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Hunt: Rare Processes</h5>
            <p><strong>Hypothesis:</strong> Malware often uses unusual process names that are rare in the
                environment.</p>
            <pre><code># Splunk - Find rare processes

index=windows EventCode=4688 | stats count by New_Process_Name | where count < 5 | sort count | head 50 

        <div class="hunt-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Hunt: Beaconing Detection</h5>
            <p><strong>Hypothesis:</strong> C2 beacons maintain regular check-in intervals.</p>
            <p><span class="mitre-tactic">Command & Control</span> <span class="mitre-technique">T1071 - Application
                    Layer Protocol</span></p>
            <pre><code># Splunk - Detect regular connection intervals

index=network | bin _time span=1m | stats count by src_ip, dest_ip, _time | streamstats window=60 stdev(count) as std, avg(count) as avg by src_ip, dest_ip | where std < 2 AND count > 50 # Low variance = beaconing | table src_ip, dest_ip, std, avg, count 

        <h3>Technique 4: Baseline Comparison</h3>
        <p>Compare current activity against known-good baselines.</p>

        <div class="hunt-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Hunt: New Scheduled Tasks</h5>
            <p><strong>Hypothesis:</strong> Attackers create scheduled tasks for persistence.</p>
            <p><span class="mitre-tactic">Persistence</span> <span class="mitre-technique">T1053.005 - Scheduled
                    Task</span></p>
            <pre><code># Splunk - New scheduled tasks in last 24h

index=windows EventCode=4698 | where _time > relative_time(now(), “-24h”) | table _time, host, TaskName, user, Task_Content | outputlookup known_scheduled_tasks.csv

Compare against baseline

| inputlookup known_scheduled_tasks_baseline.csv | append [search index=windows EventCode=4698 | where _time > relative_time(now(), “-24h”)] | stats count by TaskName | where count == 1 # New tasks only 

        <h2>4. High-Value Hunting Areas</h2>

        <p>Focus your hunts where attackers commonly operate:</p>

        <h3>Persistence Mechanisms</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Scheduled Tasks:</strong> <code>schtasks</code>, Task Scheduler events</li>
            <li><strong>Services:</strong> New service creation (Event ID 7045)</li>
            <li><strong>Registry Run Keys:</strong> <code>HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run</code>
            </li>
            <li><strong>Startup Folder:</strong>
                <code>%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup</code>
            </li>
            <li><strong>WMI Subscriptions:</strong> Permanent event consumers</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Credential Access</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>LSASS Access:</strong> Processes reading LSASS memory (Mimikatz)</li>
            <li><strong>SAM/NTDS.dit Access:</strong> Credential database theft</li>
            <li><strong>Kerberoasting:</strong> Unusual TGS requests</li>
            <li><strong>DCSync:</strong> Replication requests from non-DCs</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Lateral Movement</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>PsExec/SMB:</strong> Remote service creation, admin share access</li>
            <li><strong>WMI:</strong> Remote process creation via WMI</li>
            <li><strong>RDP:</strong> Unusual RDP connections, especially internal</li>
            <li><strong>Pass-the-Hash:</strong> Type 3 logons with NTLMv2</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Data Exfiltration</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Large Transfers:</strong> Unusual bytes out to external IPs</li>
            <li><strong>Cloud Storage:</strong> Connections to Dropbox, Google Drive, Mega</li>
            <li><strong>DNS Tunneling:</strong> Long DNS queries, high query volume</li>
            <li><strong>Archive Creation:</strong> RAR, ZIP creation in sensitive directories</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>5. Building a Hunting Program</h2>

        <h3>Prerequisites</h3>
        <p>You can't hunt without visibility:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Log collection:</strong> Endpoint, network, authentication, application</li>
            <li><strong>Centralized SIEM:</strong> Searchable, fast, with sufficient retention</li>
            <li><strong>Baseline knowledge:</strong> What's normal in your environment</li>
            <li><strong>Threat intelligence:</strong> Current threat landscape awareness</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Hunt Cadence</h3>
        <table style="width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
            <tr style="background: var(--bg-card);">
                <th style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border); color: var(--accent-blue);">Frequency
                </th>
                <th style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border); color: var(--accent-blue);">Hunt Type
                </th>
                <th style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border); color: var(--accent-blue);">Example
                </th>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Daily</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">IOC sweeps</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">New threat intel indicators</td>
            </tr>
            <tr style="background: var(--bg-card);">
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Weekly</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">TTP-based hunts</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">PowerShell abuse, persistence</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Monthly</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Deep dives</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Full ATT&CK technique coverage</td>
            </tr>

                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Ad-hoc</td>

        <h3>Hunt Documentation Template</h3>
        <pre><code>HUNT: [Descriptive Name]

DATE: [Date] HUNTER: [Analyst Name] ATT&CK: [Tactic] / [Technique ID]

HYPOTHESIS: [Clear statement of what you’re looking for and why]

DATA SOURCES:

  • [Source 1]
  • [Source 2]

QUERIES: [Include all queries used]

FINDINGS: ☐ True Positive - [Description] ☐ False Positive - [Why it triggered, tuning needed] ☐ No Findings - [Hypothesis not supported]

RECOMMENDATIONS:

  • [Detection rule improvements]

  • [Visibility gaps identified]

  • [Follow-up hunts needed]

          <h2>6. Tools for Threat Hunting</h2>

      <h3>Data Analysis</h3>
      <ul>
          <li><strong>Splunk:</strong> Enterprise SIEM with powerful SPL</li>
          <li><strong>Elastic Stack:</strong> Open-source, flexible</li>
          <li><strong>Microsoft Sentinel:</strong> Cloud-native, KQL queries</li>
          <li><strong>Jupyter Notebooks:</strong> Python-based analysis</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>Hunting Platforms</h3>
      <ul>
          <li><strong>HELK:</strong> Hunting ELK with Kafka, great for labs</li>
          <li><strong>Velociraptor:</strong> Endpoint visibility and hunting</li>
          <li><strong>OSQuery:</strong> SQL-like queries against endpoints</li>
          <li><strong>Chainsaw:</strong> Windows event log analysis</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>Threat Intelligence</h3>
      <ul>
          <li><strong>MITRE ATT&CK Navigator:</strong> Visualize technique coverage</li>
          <li><strong>MISP:</strong> Threat intel platform</li>
          <li><strong>OpenCTI:</strong> Open-source cyber threat intelligence</li>
      </ul>

      <h2>7. My Hunting Tips</h2>

      <div class="callout success">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb" style="color: var(--accent-cyan);"></i> Lessons from the
              Hunt:</strong>
          <ol>
              <li><strong>Start with what you know.</strong> Hunt in areas where you have good visibility.</li>
              <li><strong>Document everything.</strong> Even "no findings" is valuable data.</li>
              <li><strong>Think like an attacker.</strong> What would you do after getting initial access?</li>
              <li><strong>Baseline first.</strong> You can't find anomalies without knowing normal.</li>
              <li><strong>Automate your wins.</strong> Turn successful hunts into detection rules.</li>
              <li><strong>Collaborate.</strong> Share findings with your team and the community.</li>
              <li><strong>Don't get discouraged.</strong> Most hunts find nothing—that's expected.</li>
              <li><strong>Stay curious.</strong> The best hunters never stop learning.</li>
          </ol>
      </div>

      <h2>Conclusion</h2>

      <p>Threat hunting is the evolution of security from passive defense to active pursuit. It requires deep
          technical skills, creative thinking, and relentless curiosity. Not every hunt will find a threat, but
          every hunt makes you a better defender.</p>

      <p><strong>The adversaries are already in your network. Go find them.</strong></p>
